ko.title: KOSPI vs KOSDAQ: 2,764 Korean Stocks Measured Side by Side

narrative.heading: KOSPI vs KOSDAQ: the short answer, in numbers
narrative.body: KOSPI vs KOSDAQ comes down to this: both are boards of the same exchange, the Korea Exchange (KRX), but KOSPI holds the large, older companies and KOSDAQ holds the smaller, younger ones. At the close on October 23, 2026, we counted 940 stock listings on KOSPI worth ₩4,582 trillion (about $3.45 trillion at ₩1,326.6 per dollar) and 1,824 on KOSDAQ worth ₩426 trillion (about $321 billion). So KOSDAQ has nearly twice as many listings and less than a tenth of the value. Every number in this guide comes from that list of all 2,764 listings (common and preferred shares, excluding ETFs and ETNs), priced at the Korea Exchange's regular-session close and matched against our own company database. Most comparisons you will find stop at the definitions. This one measures what the boards actually hold.

narrative.heading: KOSPI is the main board, and two chipmakers now carry it
narrative.body: KOSPI is Korea's main board. A company applying to list there must have been operating for at least three years, a rule Baker McKenzie's listing guide (updated February 1, 2026) and PwC's listing summary both state; PwC also lists a shareholders' equity floor of ₩30 billion. The bar is built for maturity, and it shows: the median founding year of a KOSPI company in our data is 1977. The bigger story in October 2026 is concentration. Samsung Electronics' common shares alone were 27.5% of KOSPI's total value on October 23, and the ten largest listings were 61.9%. Companies classed as semiconductors and electronic components under Korea's standard industry codes made up 54.8%. Together with SK Hynix, the two memory makers were 47.9% of the board: when a foreign investor says "I bought Korea," nearly half of that is two companies.

narrative.heading: KOSDAQ is the growth board, and four in ten of its companies lose money
narrative.body: KOSDAQ opened in July 1996 as Korea's market for younger, faster-growing companies, and it does not require the three-year operating history KOSPI does. A technology-growth route lets a company list with as little as ₩1 billion of equity or a ₩9 billion market value (Baker McKenzie, February 2026). That shows up in the numbers. The median KOSDAQ listing was worth ₩69.0 billion on October 23, against ₩210.4 billion on KOSPI, and 62% of KOSDAQ listings were worth less than ₩100 billion. The median founding year is 2000. Using each company's latest reported return on equity in our database, 42.9% of KOSDAQ companies had a negative ROE, meaning they lost money over their last reported year, against 25.8% on KOSPI. KOSDAQ is also far less top-heavy. Its largest company, the biotech Alteogen, was 3.7% of the board, and its ten largest were 17.5%. The biggest groups by number of companies are semiconductors and components (251), software and games (185), machinery (184) and pharmaceuticals (133).

narrative.heading: Who owns each board, and how often it trades
narrative.body: Foreign investors sit mostly on KOSPI. Weighted by company size, overseas investors held 38.5% of KOSPI on our latest readings, against 11.3% of KOSDAQ. For the typical (median) company the gap is smaller but still clear: 5.0% foreign-held on KOSPI and 2.4% on KOSDAQ. KOSDAQ makes up for its size with turnover. On October 23, KOSPI traded ₩17.0 trillion, about 0.37% of its value, while KOSDAQ traded ₩5.8 trillion, about 1.36% of its value. Relative to size, KOSDAQ shares changed hands roughly 3.7 times as often that day. That is one day, not an average, so treat it as a snapshot.

narrative.heading: Which board swings more? In 2026, the answer depends on what you hold
narrative.body: The usual rule is that KOSDAQ is the volatile board. Our autumn 2026 data only half agrees. From August 28 to October 23, 2026, KOSPI fell from 6,788.88 to 5,550.30, a drop of 18.2%, while KOSDAQ fell from 838.41 to 751.69, a drop of 10.3%. Across the 34 sessions in that window for which we hold closing prices confirmed by two sources, KOSPI moved 3% or more in a day nine times and KOSDAQ six times. On October 15 they fell together, KOSPI by 7.57% and KOSDAQ by 7.65%. The reason is the concentration above. An index that is more than half chipmakers moves like a chip stock. Single stocks still follow the old rule, though: on October 23, 9.3% of KOSDAQ listings moved 5% or more in one session, against 6.8% on KOSPI. So if you buy the KOSPI index, your risk is how much rides on Samsung and SK Hynix. If you buy an individual KOSDAQ name, your risk is the company itself.

narrative.heading: How to tell which board a Korean stock is on
narrative.body: Korean tickers are six-digit numbers on both boards, so the number alone does not tell you. The suffix does. On Yahoo Finance and many data terminals, .KS means KOSPI and .KQ means KOSDAQ: Samsung Electronics is 005930.KS and Alteogen is 196170.KQ. Your broker's quote page will also name the board directly. Boards are not permanent. Large KOSDAQ companies sometimes move to KOSPI, and a stock's board can change what index funds hold it, so check the label again before relying on an old note.

narrative.heading: What we could and could not verify
narrative.body:
We took the listing counts, share counts and trading values from the full KOSPI and KOSDAQ lists published on Naver Finance, and priced every listing at the regular-session close of October 23, 2026, from our own snapshot of Korea Exchange closing prices taken at 15:33 KST. That matters: the list's own prices include evening trading after 15:30, which moved some stocks by a percent or more. Thirty-one listings, mostly suspended issues, were missing from the snapshot and keep the list price. The board totals match the change in both indices since the Korea Exchange's September 14 figures (₩5,567.1 trillion for KOSPI and ₩455.1 trillion for KOSDAQ) to within 1%. Index closes come from our own daily files, which accept a close only when two independent sources agree. Three trading days in the window (September 1, 28 and 29) are missing from those files, so the count of big-move days covers 34 of 37 sessions.

Return on equity and foreign ownership come from our company database, refreshed on a rolling basis; the readings used here are from October 16 to October 23, 2026. Industry groups follow Korea's standard industry classification (KSIC) as recorded in company filings. We did not check the current KRX rulebook line by line; the listing thresholds above come from Baker McKenzie and PwC summaries, and the exchange can change them.

closing.heading: The takeaway
closing.body:
Check the board before you check anything else, but read it correctly. KOSDAQ tells you the company is probably small, young and more likely to be losing money. KOSPI tells you the company is probably large and established, and in 2026 it also tells you that the index itself is mostly a bet on memory chips.

All figures are as of the close on October 23, 2026, unless stated otherwise, and they change daily. This guide is for information only and is not investment advice.
